slides.title: Graphs: traversals and connectivity
slides.main: A tree is just a graph with no cycles and one root; today, the general case.

captions: A tree is a graph without cycles, with one root
Add an edge between "cousins": a cycle appears
Graph: vertices and edges; edges may be directed (arrows), weighted or not

slides.title: Storage: matrix and lists
slides.sub: The first decision: where to put the graph
slides.main: Dense graphs live in a matrix, sparse ones in lists; most real systems are sparse.

captions: Four vertices, four edges
n × n matrix: edge check is O(1), but memory is always n², even when sparse
Lists: each vertex has its neighbors; memory O(V + E), neighbor scan is instant

slides.title: Depth-first search
slides.sub: Dive into the first unvisited neighbor, back up at a dead end
slides.main: One full traversal visits every vertex and edge: O(V + E), the basic operation of the chapter.

captions: Dive into the first unvisited neighbor
Dead end at D: step back
From B, take the next branch: to E
A visited set is needed, or cycles loop forever
All vertices visited; time O(V + E)

frames.text: back at B, dive into E
order: A B D E C F G

slides.title: Connectivity and cycles
slides.main: The number of traversal runs equals the number of connected components.

captions: The graph split into two islands
The first run visited one island
An unvisited vertex starts run two; runs = components
Connectivity, component count, cycle search: all in O(V + E)

slides.title: Three colors: an exact cycle detector
slides.main: Three colors are the industry standard; write the detector once and never be confused again.

captions: White: untouched; gray: dive in progress; black: vertex and subtree done
Walk P → Q → R → S: the whole chain is gray
S points to gray Q: back in our own current path, a cycle
An edge to a black vertex is harmless: that branch is finished, no ring

frames.text: gray = on the path, black = finished

slides.title: Topological sort
slides.main: Unload the answer stack, and dependencies always come first.

captions: Dependency graph: an arrow means "must be done earlier"; no cycles
A task goes to the answer once all its dependencies are done: E, D, B, C, A
Unload the stack in reverse: A C B D E, dependencies first

frames.text: exit order: E D B C A
reverse order: A C B D E

slides.title: Kahn's algorithm
slides.main: If the answer is shorter than the vertex list, the rest sit in a cycle.

captions: In-degree = number of dependencies; zero means do it now
A removed: B and C drop to zero and join the queue
B and C cleared D's dependencies: D drops to zero
Queue empty; fewer vertices in the answer than in the graph means a cycle. O(V + E)

frames.text: queue: D   answer: A B C
queue: —   answer: A B C D E

slides.title: Breadth-first search: waves
slides.sub: No diving, we spread in waves
slides.main: The number of waves to a vertex is the shortest path length in an unweighted graph.

captions: A queue with one vertex; waves will spread in circles
Wave one: the immediate neighbors B and C
Wave two: neighbors of neighbors: D, E, F
Wave three: G. Distance = wave number: shortest paths when unweighted

slides.title: Uses of BFS
slides.sub: Wherever edges are alike and fewest steps matter
slides.main: Equal edges and fewest steps: breadth-first is the right answer, no complications.

captions: Each vertex remembers where it came from (parent) and its distance
The path is rebuilt via parents from goal to start: G ← E ← B ← A
A vertex can be any state: a knight's square, a word, a game position

slides.title: Depth versus breadth
slides.main: Any path, fast: depth; the shortest path: breadth.

captions: Cells are vertices, passages are edges; get from S to G
Depth gets there fast, but the path winds: 15 cells
Breadth floods in waves; the first path to arrive is shortest: 13 cells

slides.title: Six handshakes
slides.sub: BFS on the graph of humanity
slides.main: Seeing the world as waves saves weeks of reinventing.

captions: You are the center of the wave
Wave one: friends
Wave two: friends of friends; the count grows exponentially
Six waves cover almost everyone: handshakes are breadth-first search

slides.title: Bipartite coloring
slides.sub: Color by waves: neighbors get the opposite color
slides.main: One traversal, one color array, and a non-trivial answer about the graph.

captions: Color by waves, opposite for neighbors; the square can be colored
In a triangle two neighbors get the same color: impossible
An odd cycle blocks bipartiteness; success means two conflict-free teams

slides.title: Implementation pitfalls
slides.main: Deep recursion and queue duplicates are the two most common traversal bugs.

captions: Recursion on a million vertices blows the stack: write it iteratively
Mark visited on enqueue, not on dequeue, or duplicates appear
Remember the parent: it rebuilds the path
One run covers one component: start from every unvisited vertex

slides.title: A grid as a graph
slides.main: Spot the vertices and adjacency, and the familiar traversals do the rest.

captions: Land and water: a cell is a vertex
Edges are vertical and horizontal contacts
Each unvisited land cell starts a traversal marking its island: 3 islands, 3 runs

slides.title: Bridges and articulation points
slides.main: Reliability questions are solved by the same depth-first search you now know well.

captions: Two dense groups joined by a single link
A bridge is an edge whose loss splits the graph; a cut point is a vertex like that
One modified DFS finds them all in O(V + E): which server is critical, what to back up
